newsitem.title: USA: Calif. agency urges funding plan for projects.
newsitem.headline: Calif. agency urges funding plan for projects.

text.p: The California legislative analyst's office urged the state legislature on Wednesday not to approve any capital outlay project without a specific plan for funding future completion costs.

In a detailed review of the $67 billion 1997/98 state budget proposed last month by California's Republican Gov. Pete Wilson, the legislative analyst's office said the Wilson administration had not identified funding sources for $800 million in future costs of projects proposed in the budget.

"The legislature should not approve any capital outlay project unless there is a specific plan for funding the future completion costs," the legislative analyst's office, a non-partisan agency which advises the state legislature, said in the report.

The analyst's office said the state legislature should also consider "a multipurpose state facilities bond act for the June 1998 ballot in order to finance the state's highest priority capital outlay needs."
The Democratic-dominated state legislature will discuss Wilson's budget proposal and should pass a budget before the start of the 1997/98 fiscal year on July 1.
The legislative analyst's office estimated that adoption of Wilson's budget proposal would result in a General Fund reserve of $768 million in 1997/98, $214 million higher than Wilson's estimate.

The agency said its higher reserve estimate took account of its higher estimate of revenues, its lower estimate of health and welfare caseloads and its lower assumption of state savings that are reliant on federal actions.
Wilson has proposed far-reaching changes to the state welfare system, including limits on how long people may remain on welfare and cuts in grants after a certain period.

The legislative analyst's office estimated that the caseload for the Aid to Families with Dependent Children and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families programs would fall more sharply than projected in Wilson's budget.
"This would result in General Fund savings of $117 million in 1996/97 and $161 million in 1997/98, compared to (Wilson's) budget," it said.

The analyst's office also noted that Wilson's budget proposal includes $484 million in General Fund savings in health and social services programs that required federal legislation. "To the extent the required legislation is not forthcoming, there will be a budgetary hole in these programs," it said.
The report also said that seismic retrofit of state-owned toll bridges faced a $1.4 billion funding gap and a funding solution was needed in 1997/98 for retrofit to proceed.
"We recommend that the legislature enact a funding solution consisting of a mix of toll bridge revenues and State Highway Account funds," the legislative analyst's office said.
